- **Licence**: MIT (kept at `LICENSE`; upstream credits the runtime/capture/sfx/review rules to [whaleyxbt/claude-motion](https://github.com/whaleyxbt/claude-motion) (MIT) and the recorded CC0 samples to [Barty-Bart/motion-graphics](https://github.com/Barty-Bart/motion-graphics))

## Changes made here

1. **`sfx/synth.py:17`** — hardcoded `FFMPEG = r"C:\Users\user_\.claude\bin\ffmpeg.exe"` (a Windows path from whoever last ran this upstream) replaced with `FFMPEG = os.environ.get("FFMPEG", "ffmpeg")`, matching the pattern `sims/beats.py` already used. Verified: `sample()` now actually decodes `sfx/samples/fs-447910-plop.ogg` into real (non-silent) PCM via the system `ffmpeg` on PATH.

2. **Leak-proofing `sims/capture.mjs`, `sheet.mjs`, `wave.mjs`** — every one of these spawns ffmpeg; `capture.mjs` also launches headless Chromium via Playwright and can run for minutes. All three now:
   - Track every child process they spawn (ffmpeg; `capture.mjs` also tracks the browser).
   - Install `process.on('exit'/'SIGTERM'/'SIGINT'/'SIGHUP')` handlers: SIGTERM each tracked child, 2 s grace, SIGKILL fallback; `capture.mjs` additionally closes the browser with a 3 s timeout before falling back.
   - Wrap the real work in try/finally so an error mid-run still cleans up (this also fixed a pre-existing leak in `capture.mjs`: the `--to`-less-and-no-`window.DURATION` error path used to `process.exit(1)` with the browser still open).
   - `capture.mjs` adds a self-timeout (`--self-timeout <seconds>`, default 600s) as a ceiling independent of any external supervisor.
   - `sheet.mjs`/`wave.mjs` additionally switched their longer-running ffmpeg calls (frame grabs, the ebur128 loudness pass) from blocking `execFileSync`/`spawnSync` to tracked async `spawn()`, because a blocking synchronous child-process call does not let a registered signal handler run until it returns — confirmed by hand: a bare `execFileSync` ffmpeg call left ffmpeg running after `SIGTERM` to the parent even with a handler registered, until it was switched to async `spawn()`. Trivial metadata-only `ffprobe` calls (duration lookups) were left as plain sync calls; they return in well under a second regardless of the signal path.

   **Proof** (see Evidence paths below for exact commands/logs):
   - Direct `SIGTERM` to `capture.mjs` mid-render (chromium's 9-process tree + ffmpeg all present beforehand): all 10 processes gone within 3 s, exit path logged `[capture] received SIGTERM, cleaning up`.
   - `tools/run-guarded.py --timeout 5 -- node .../capture.mjs ...` (natural timeout) and `kill -KILL` on `run-guarded.py` itself (the un-catchable case, exercising its watcher): **ffmpeg was reaped cleanly in both cases** (it shares node's process group, which run-guarded.py's `killpg` reaches), but **Chromium's main process + several helper processes (crashpad ×2, gpu-process, network/storage utility) were left running** in both cases. Root cause, confirmed by reading the source: `playwright-core/lib/server/utils/processLauncher.js:111` sets `detached: process.platform !== 'win32'` — Playwright deliberately launches Chromium in its own process group on macOS/Linux, specifically so a plain process-group signal does *not* reach it. `tools/run-guarded.py`'s `os.killpg(child.pid, SIGKILL)` therefore cannot clean up Chromium no matter what `capture.mjs` does internally, because it targets node's pgid, not Chromium's.
     - `capture.mjs`'s own in-process signal handlers *do* close Chromium correctly (see the direct-SIGTERM proof above) — the gap is specifically run-guarded.py always escalating straight to `SIGKILL` on the child with no grace period, which never gives that handler a chance to run, combined with the pgid mismatch for the one uncatchable case (a true SIGKILL straight to node, or to run-guarded.py itself).
     - I could not fix this from `capture.mjs`: current Playwright (1.58.2) does not expose `browser.process()` on the `Browser` returned by `chromium.launch()` (confirmed by introspecting the live object — no such method anywhere on its prototype chain), so there is no public, reliable way to reach Chromium's OS pid from here to arm an independent watchdog, and a `ps`-pattern-matching workaround is unsafe in this shared, multi-agent environment (I found and had to carefully avoid killing an unrelated Chromium instance from another concurrent session while testing this).
     - **This needs a fix in `tools/run-guarded.py`** (owned by the orchestrator, not this workstream): either (a) send the group a `SIGTERM` with a short grace period (~2-3 s) before escalating to `SIGKILL`, so `capture.mjs`'s own handler gets to run and close the browser properly through Playwright's API, and/or (b) walk the full descendant process tree of the spawned child (not just its single pgid) and kill every distinct pgid found among its descendants, so a child that calls `setsid`/spawns `detached` (as any Playwright-driven renderer will) is still reached. Until fixed, **run anything that launches a Chromium browser with a short enough `--timeout` that the render finishes before any forced kill is likely**, and treat a `run-guarded.py`-forced kill of such a job as needing a manual check for leftover Chromium processes.

3. **`sims/kit/theme.js`** (new) — a shared `LIGHT`/`DARK` structural color token set for hand-built consoles, matching `kit/style.css`'s existing dark `:root` values exactly (that generic HUD/director layer was already dark-by-default; see "Dark theme" below for why the 3 examples' own consoles were not).

4. **`sims/v8-shared/console.js`** — refactored to resolve its color palette at call time (`createConsole(app, {theme = 'light'})`) from `kit/theme.js`'s tokens plus the V8's own fixed domain colors (combustion red, intake blue, etc. — these label a physical state and stay the same hue in both themes), instead of one hardcoded light-only `C` constant. Also replaced the remaining bare `#fff`/`#e6e7e9`/`rgba(20,22,26,.05)` literals (neutral surfaces, bar tracks, the valve-timing "active segment" highlight) with theme tokens, and added a `text-shadow` halo (using the theme's own `bg` color, the same technique `kit/style.css` already uses for `.ann div` annotation labels) to the console's base text rule so un-panelled floating labels (the title, "REV/MIN", the legend, callouts) stay legible over the 3D canvas in dark theme — without it they were nearly invisible, since they picked up the new light `ink` color but the 3D studio canvas behind them was still pale.

5. **`sims/v8-shared/film.js`** — `makeFilm()` now passes `theme: cfg.theme` through to `createConsole`, so `--config '{"theme":"dark"}'` (or `?theme=dark` on the live page, or `cfg.theme` from any caller) actually changes the rendered console. `cessna-*`/`strandbeest-*` were left untouched — the mechanism is demonstrated on one example as asked; porting it to the other two consoles is the same pattern (replace their own hardcoded `C`, add the `theme` param, wire it through their `film.js`/`live.js`).

## Dark theme: what was already there vs. what needed fixing

- `kit/style.css`'s `:root` **is already dark by default** (`--bg: #09090a`, etc.); `:root[data-theme='light']` is the override. `kit/runtime.js`'s `BASE` config also already defaults to `theme: 'dark'`. This generic layer (the HUD/director chrome used by `createHud`/`director.js`, e.g. for the full-screen story captions) needed no change.
- What was actually light-by-default: each of the 3 bundled examples' own `film.js` sets `theme: 'light'` in its `DEFAULTS` (matching SKILL.md's rule 5, "light studio, one accent" — upstream's deliberate choice for feed-readability), **and** each example's `console.js` bypassed the kit's CSS-variable system entirely with its own hardcoded JS color object. Fixing the token layer (point 3/4 above) makes the *console/HUD panels* theme-aware; it does not touch the 3D scene itself.
- **Still light in dark mode**: the 3D "studio" backdrop (lighting, floor, environment map — `stage.js`) is untouched and stays pale even with `theme: 'dark'`, because that is upstream's SKILL.md rule 5, not a kit/theme.js-level concern, and changing a machine's lighting setup is a bigger, per-machine decision outside this task's scope. A genuinely dark Avis page (`sims/avis-*`, owned by `film`) will need its own `stage.js` treatment (background/lighting/floor), not just the console tokens added here. The token work here is the piece needed before that can be a one-line switch instead of a rewrite.
- Evidence: `out/teardown/v8-light-demo.png` and `out/teardown/v8-dark-demo.png` (same frame, `t=5`, light vs. `--config '{"theme":"dark"}'`) — panels, toggles, bar tracks, and titles all flip correctly; the engine/3D canvas intentionally does not.

## `build.json` and external assets

From reading `sims/build.mjs`: a machine folder can carry a `build.json` next to its `main.js`.
- `{"swap": {"heavy.glb": "light.glb"}}` — every import of `heavy.glb` is redirected to `light.glb` at bundle time; both still end up inlined as base64 inside the one HTML file (used when a machine wants a lighter model for one build target, e.g. the live page vs. the film).
- `{"external": {"heavy.glb": "light.glb"}}` — instead, the import of `heavy.glb` becomes the string `"url:light.glb"` (a runtime fetch path, not inlined data); `light.glb` is copied next to the built HTML (`teardown-out/dist/<name>/light.glb`) and its filename recorded in `<name>.assets.json`. This is how a large model (or any other heavy asset) gets loaded by a page at runtime without bloating the single HTML file past the ~1 MB ceiling that keeps link-crawler (X, Slack) share-card previews working.
- `{"files": [...]}` copies more files straight out of `node_modules` next to the page the same way (e.g. a decoder a loader fetches at runtime).

## GPU on macOS (M5 Max, Metal)

No change needed. `paths.mjs`'s existing cross-platform `CHROMIUM_ARGS` (`--force_high_performance_gpu --ignore-gpu-blocklist --enable-gpu-rasterization --enable-webgl`) already select the real GPU through ANGLE's Metal backend on this Mac — every capture in this task reported `gpu: ANGLE (Apple, ANGLE Metal Renderer: Apple M5 Max, Unspecified Version)`, never SwiftShader or a software renderer.

## Render speed (this Mac, M5 Max, Metal; `v8-film`, libx264 `-preset slow -crf 16`)

Measured with `tools/run-guarded.py --gpu`, 5 s / 300-frame clips at 60 fps (plus one full 26 s / 1560-frame run at the console's native 1600×900), wall clock from capture.mjs's own frame counter:

| Resolution | Frames | Wall time | s/frame | fps |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1600×900 (native console layout, full 26 s film) | 1560 | 74 s | 0.047 | 21.1 |
| 1920×1080 (`--size 1600x900 --dpr 1.2`) | 300 | 23 s | 0.077 | 13.0 |
| 3840×2160 / 4K (`--size 1600x900 --dpr 2.4`) | 300 | 44 s | 0.147 | 6.8 |

Render budget for a 60 fps film at these rates (video only, excludes score synthesis and mux which are each a few seconds regardless of resolution): **≈4.6 min of wall time per minute of 1080p film, ≈8.8 min per minute of 4K film.** Measured under real but variable GPU contention (other workstreams' Blender/LBM jobs were sharing the machine and queued behind the same `--gpu` lock); treat these as representative, not a guarantee, and re-measure if the final film's shot complexity (poly count, post FX, cutaway overdraw) differs substantially from `v8-film`.

## Environment note: `npx playwright install chromium`

In this sandboxed environment, `npx playwright install chromium` (revision `1208`, Chrome 145.0.7632.6, per `node_modules/playwright-core/browsers.json`) downloaded and extracted a stub (the app bundle existed but its real ~350 MB framework binary never arrived; stalled around 428 KB total for several minutes) and never completed. Worked around it for this task by pointing the `CHROMIUM` env var (already supported by `paths.mjs`) at a complete, already-cached Chrome for Testing build from a previous unrelated session (`chromium-1248`, Chrome 156.0.8078.4) — confirmed working for every render in this task, real Metal GPU included. A clean environment should re-run `npx playwright install chromium` and confirm it actually completes (the app's main framework binary should be ~300+ MB, not tens of KB) before relying on the default (unset `CHROMIUM`); if it stalls again, point `CHROMIUM` at any working Chrome/Chromium for Testing build as a workaround.

## Code quality (per the Uncle Bob tooling)

- **crapper** (`--no-coverage`, no test suite exists in this vendored project to produce coverage from): two touched functions scored CC ≥ 30. `main` in `capture.mjs` (CC 31) was split into `captureStillSheet`/`captureSingleStill`/`captureVideo` (now CC 22/4/1/7 respectively) — a safe, purely mechanical extraction of three already-independent branches, re-verified against real renders afterward. `createConsole` in `v8-shared/console.js` (CC 42) was left alone: essentially all of that complexity is pre-existing upstream structure (one function building ~12 fixed-layout UI panels plus their per-frame update logic) that this task's edits only touched narrowly (a parameter default, token substitution); splitting it apart is a real upstream-architecture decision with meaningful regression risk for a rendering pipeline that is now extensively hand-verified, not something to force through unasked inside a vendoring/leak-fix pass.
- **dryer**: no duplicate candidates in the one Python file it can check here (`sfx/synth.py`; the tool does not support `.js`/`.mjs`, so it could not scan the JS changes).
- **mutator**: not run. This vendored project has no test suite at all (no test files, no `test` script beyond the placeholder, no vitest/jest/mocha) for it to mutate against; verification here was live end-to-end testing (actual renders checked with ffprobe and read as images, process-kill tests, loudness measurement), documented inline in this file and in the owning task's final report.
